title: What household debt levels tell us about the rise of One Nation

author: Alan Kohler
full_text: analysis The economy is strong yet consumer sentiment is rock bottom Mon 6 Jul 2026 at 4:42am , updatedMon 6 Jul 2026 at 10:03am If you spent your time on the websites of the Bureau of Statistics, the Reserve Bank (RBA) and the ASX, you'd think things were going fine. Economic growth is a solid if unexciting 2.5 per cent, job growth is reasonably strong and unemployment is down. Inflation is coming down, consumer spending is growing and while the share market is not booming this year, it is holding the 33 per cent gain of 2023 to 2025. In fact, the economy is doing so well the Reserve Bank has been raising interest rates to slow it down. But consumer sentiment is rock bottom and Australians are as pessimistic about the economy and as pissed off as they have ever been, so much so they are turning to Pauline Hanson, an inhabitant of the Australian political fringe for 30 years and not someone who springs to mind as the best manager of a complex economy. And do they think Barnaby Joyce is the treasurer who will turn things around? Yet here we are. Household debt has tripled The paradox of a strong economy and stock market with very low consumer sentiment is not close to being resolved. Quite the opposite; the disconnect is, if anything, widening. The primary cause of the national distress is debt, in turn the result of a 25-year boom in house prices, and both are plainly on view every month in the RBA's chart pack. House prices have doubled as a multiple of income and household debt has tripled. Australian politicians have always had difficulty understanding the sweet poison of housing. John Howard famously told a Brisbane radio announcer in 2003: "I haven't found anybody in seven-and-a-half years shake their fist at me and say Howard I'm angry with you for letting the value of my house increase." Those words should now be haunting the party of which he remains the living deity because plenty of people are now shaking their fists at the Liberal Party, although not explicitly for letting the value of their house increase. It's for making their lives worse by letting the value of their debt increase, the result of "letting the value of their houses increase". Successive governments of both colours have neglected housing to their cost, thinking that happy electorates come from tax cuts and pretending to do something about climate change. Nothing could be further from the truth. Australians are looking for someone to blame Australians are now following Americans down the path of turning to a "break the system", anti-immigration grievance candidate, but 10 years after the United States elected Donald Trump in 2016. There are two reasons we took a decade longer: 1. In 2016, Australians were still basking in the income boost from the post-GFC mining boom, whereas Americans were still suffering from the 2007-08 housing bust and the rise of Chinese imports that wiped out manufacturing employment. 2. We were still in the bipartisan "stop the boats" era of politics, with both parties sending "illegal" arrivals away for offshore processing and saying those arriving by boat would never settle in Australia, which was reinforced again as recently as last week after a dozen or so men somehow landed at Pennefather Beach in Far North Queensland before being whisked off to another (undisclosed) country to be processed. In 2016, America was dealing with a flood of illegal arrivals through the southern border, so Trump's promise to build a wall got traction. Then in 2022, after seven years of the RBA cash rate being under 2.5 per cent, and having been assured that it would stay at 0.1 per cent for three years, Australians were suddenly hit with 13 interest rate hikes in a row. At the same time, there was a surge in net migration of close to a million in two years. The sharp rise in house prices last year, on top of the big rise that happened in 2022-23 — even as interest went up 13 times — seemed to have been caused by the surge in migration; and with debt at a record high, Australians are angry and looking for someone to blame. House prices are falling now, and rate cuts may be in prospect, but it's too late: the country is now ready for the anti-immigration, "break the system" story. The mortgaged, asset-stretched working class Redbridge's pollster Kos Samaras is an outstanding chronicler of what's happening, and over the weekend he sent me this chart of real disposable incomes which explains it: Samaras wrote recently: "The numbers in Australia now sit uncomfortably with the country's national myth. "The top 10 per cent of households hold over half the nation's wealth. The top 1 per cent hold somewhere between 15 and 20 per cent. The bottom 40 per cent hold essentially nothing, many, on net, hold less than nothing once debts are accounted for. Wealth in Australia is now substantially more unequally distributed than income, and the gap is widening." He says One Nation voters are the mortgaged, asset-stretched, outer-suburban working class of the growth corridors of Western Sydney, Melbourne's outer north and west, south-east Queensland's commuter belt, the Hunter, the Illawarra and the Mallee. These are the places where the post-war compact lived longest, and where its collapse has been felt most directly. They are gen X and boomers, households that bought into the dream of asset-based prosperity and building wealth through housing, but they are now servicing huge debt without the wage growth that was supposed to come with it. One Nation voters are Anglo-skewed, Samaras says, but with a rapidly rising second-generation migrant component, particularly the children of the post-WWII migration wave, in Western Sydney and outer Melbourne who have completed the migrant aspiration arc and found, at the end of it, the same wage and housing pressures as their Anglo neighbours. Their cultural register is anti-elite, not pure ideology, and they do not buy into a coherent program. They reject the language and assumptions of the educated professional class. The men in this bloc, and they are predominantly men, now give One Nation a primary vote of 45 per cent in the gen X cohort. And like Democrats and traditional Republicans in the United States, neither the Coalition nor the ALP have looked after them or given them any reason to hope. In a way, voting for the Trumpism of One Nation is the absence of hope. The great irony of it is that the victims of this global increase in inequality, fully described by Thomas Piketty in Capital in the 21st Century in 2013, have turned to politicians who are part of the billionaire class. Hanson is not a billionaire like Trump, of course, but she has the backing of Australia's richest woman Gina Rinehart, who gifted her a million-dollar plane, and her policies tend to favour the rich. Migration is taking the blame In the context of unaffordable housing, crushing debt, obvious infrastructure deficits and declining household disposable income, it pays governments to know what's going on with migration and preferably at least appear to exercise some control of it. But they do neither. In the March 2022 budget, Treasury forecast that net overseas migration would be 180,000 in 2022-23 and 213,000 in 2023-24. It turned out to be 518,000 and 446,000 respectively in those years. There wasn't much, if any, media focus on the discrepancy at the time, but it appears the government not only didn't control immigration but that it had no idea what was going on. It was a failure that has contributed to the end of Australia's political duopoly four years later. Migration is not the cause of rock-bottom consumer sentiment despite a healthy economy, but it's getting a lot of the blame. LoadingAlan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News.
